messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 25
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Bus Driver
- Trauma Type: Military
- Pcl5: 74

She is twenty-five years old, but when she sits in the chair across from me, she looks like she is bracing for an explosion. Her name is Emily, and she has been driving a city bus for the last eighteen months. Before that, she was a mechanic in the Army, deployed to a forward operating base in eastern Afghanistan.

She tells me the story in pieces, like she is picking shrapnel out of her own skin. It happened during her second tour. She was working the night shift in the motor pool, repairing a fuel line on an MRAP. The base had been quiet for weeks. She remembers the air was dry and cold, and the stars were so sharp they looked like they could cut you. At 0230 hours, a single rocket landed inside the wire. It hit the tent next to the motor pool. She felt the concussion wave before she heard the sound—a pressure that pushed her chest inward and made her teeth ache. The blast threw her against the concrete floor. She landed on her back, and for a few seconds, she could not move. She could not hear anything except a high, thin ringing. Then she smelled it: burning rubber, diesel, and something else—something sweet and metallic that she now knows is burning human tissue.

She got up. She helped pull two soldiers from the wreckage. She held a tourniquet on a man’s leg while he screamed and told her his name was Private First Class Miller and that he had a daughter named Lily. She remembers the exact shade of red that soaked through her gloves. She remembers the heat on her face. She remembers that after it was over, someone handed her a bottle of water, and she could not make her hands stop shaking enough to open it.

She came home ten months later. The transition was not dramatic. There was no ceremony, no parade. She just took off her uniform, put on civilian clothes, and walked into a world that did not know what a rocket sounded like. She got the bus driver job because it was available and because she thought the routine would help. It did not.

Now, every day, she climbs into the driver’s seat and scans her mirrors the way she used to scan for IEDs. She checks the rearview mirror every four to five seconds, a habit she cannot break. When a car backfires outside the bus, she hits the brakes so hard that passengers complain. She has learned to anticipate the sound of a motorcycle backfiring, of a truck door slamming, of a child popping a balloon near the curb. Each sound is a trigger. Each trigger sends her back to the motor pool, to the heat, to the ringing in her ears.

She has started to avoid certain routes. She will not drive past construction sites where jackhammers are running. She will not drive near the fairgrounds when the fireworks are scheduled. She told her supervisor she has a medical condition, and he moved her to a quieter line, but she still jumps when the bus’s air brakes hiss.

At night, she cannot sleep. She lies in bed with her back to the wall, facing the door. She keeps a flashlight on her nightstand and a tactical knife under her pillow, even though she lives alone in a safe neighborhood. She has nightmares three or four times a week. In the dreams, she is back in the motor pool, but this time she is the one burning. She wakes up gasping, her sheets soaked with sweat, her heart hammering so hard she thinks she might die.

She does not talk about the war. Her friends from high school do not know she served. When someone thanks her for her service, she changes the subject. She has not told anyone about Private First Class Miller. She has not told anyone that she still feels his blood on her hands, that she can still smell the burning, that she sometimes catches herself scanning a crowded bus for threats the way she once scanned a perimeter for insurgents.

She came to see me because her sister made the appointment. Emily does not think she has a problem. She thinks she is just tired. She thinks if she can get enough sleep, she will be fine. But when I ask her to rate her distress on a scale from zero to eighty, she scores a seventy-four. She does not know what that number means, but I do. It means she is living inside a war that ended two years ago, and she cannot find the way out.
